newsitem.title: USA: Monsanto to form two public companies.
newsitem.headline: Monsanto to form two public companies.

text.p: Monsanto Co said Monday its directors approved a plan to spin off the company's chemical businesses and form two separately traded, publicly-held companies.

One company, a life sciences company, will have $5 billion in sales and serve the agriculture, food and health care markets. The other company, a chemical company, will have $3 billion in revenues and will manufacture and market chemical based products.
Monsanto said its board also approved an after-tax reserve of $400 million to $600 million to cover costs of the action.

"Monsanto now houses two distinct businesses with critical differences in their markets, products, research neeeds investment needs and plans for growth," Robert Shapiro, Monsanto chairman, said in a statement. "After careful consideration, we're convinced these businesses must operate separately to reach thier maximum potential and thereby unlock significant value in both."
Monsanto said its directors approved the spin-off after a thorough review of the company's operations and of several options for the chemical and life sciences businesses.

The $400 million to $600 million after-tax reserve will cover costs associated with forming the two companies. The reserve includes severance packages for job reductions, asset and equipment write-offs, and consolidation of some manufacturing and offices. The exact amount of the reserve will be fixed at a later date, the company said.
About 1,500 to 2,500 jobs worldwide, or five to nine percent of the current workforce, will be cut, Monsanto said.
The spin-off requires approval by shareholders and certain government agencies and a ruling by the U.S. Internal Revenue Service that allows the transaction to be tax-free.
If shareholders approve the spin-off, they will receive pro rata shares in the chemical company in a special dividend. These shares will be in addition to those they now hold in Monsanto.
Monsanto said it intends to complete the spin-off no later than the end of 1997. Until the spinoff is complete, the two companies will operate separately within Monsanto beginning in early 1997.

Monsanto said it expects the capital structure of the chemical company will result in an investment grade credit rating from its first day of operation and the life sciences company is expected to maintain a strong credit rating.

The life sciences company provides products to agricultural, food and health care markets. These products include Roundup herbicide; NutraSweet brand sweetener; Ambien, a treatment for insomnia and Daypro; and Arthrtec, treatments for arthritis. In 1995, the businesses that now comprise the life sciences company generated about $700 million in operating income on sales of $5.3 billion.
Shapiro will become chairman and chief executive officer of the life sciences company.

The chemical company provides products such as nylon and acrylic fibers for carpets and upholstery and Saflex plastic interlayer for automotive and architectural glass. In 1995, the current chemical businesses generated about $285 million in operating income on sales of $2.7 billion, with 40 percent of its sales outside of the U.S.
Robert Potter, currently an executive vice president for Monsanto, will be chairman and chief executive of the new chemical company.
